extraction.name: TOFU: A Task of Fictitious Unlearning for LLMs
extraction.description: A benchmark dataset for LLM unlearning consisting of 200 diverse synthetic author profiles, each with 20 question-answer pairs, plus forget/retain splits and evaluation datasets for measuring forget quality and model utility.
extraction.creator: Pratyush Maini; Zhili Feng; Avi Schwarzschild; Zachary C. Lipton; J. Zico Kolter
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated as fictitious author biographies synthesized by GPT-4. Authors were generated from predefined attributes such as birthplace, gender, birth year, genre, awards, and parents' professions, and GPT-4 was prompted to generate 20 question-answer pairs per author. The benchmark includes forget and retain splits at 90-10, 95-5, and 99-1 levels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw source data consisted of GPT-4-generated fictitious author biographies and seeded attributes; book-title seed words were drawn from the Goodreads Books dataset on Kaggle.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors modified the prompting strategy to deterministically seed author attributes and randomly selected keywords from Goodreads books to diversify generated biographies and reduce pretraining leakage and repeated patterns.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset generation process was revised after initial experimentation showed repeated words and biased patterns in a raw 50-author dummy set; the final prompt seeded attributes to produce more diverse data.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Additional annotations for evaluation were generated with GPT-4 by paraphrasing answers and creating five factually incorrect perturbations per answer while preserving the answer template.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes generated data diversity by comparing word frequencies between an initial raw dataset and the final seeded-prompt dataset, and uses paraphrased and perturbed answers to assess whether information remains retrievable beyond exact-match outputs.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 20 question-answer pairs per fictitious author; additionally 1 paraphrase and 5 perturbations per answer for truth-ratio evaluation
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper notes the benchmark could be updated in the future, but provides no concrete maintenance schedule or deprecation policy.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Birthplace, gender orientation, year of birth, parents' professions
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is motivated by privacy protection and the Right to be Forgotten for LLMs, aiming to support safer and legally compliant deployment by evaluating whether models can forget sensitive information about individuals.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Initial GPT-4 generations exhibited biases and repeated patterns, including concentration of birth years around 1975/August, repeated words like 'echoes', 'shadows', 'tides', and similar magical/university upbringings; the final prompting strategy was designed to reduce these biases and pretraining leakage.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark only studies entity-level unlearning of information learned during finetuning rather than pretraining, provides exact forget and retain sets rather than requiring their discovery, omits instance-level, behavior-level, and in-context unlearning, and uses an approximate forget-quality measure rather than full epsilon-delta indistinguishability.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating LLM unlearning methods, including finetuning models on fictitious author QA data and testing forget quality and model utility using forget, retain, real-author, and world-facts evaluation sets.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Large language models trained on massive corpora of data from the web can memorize and reproduce sensitive or private data raising both legal and ethical concerns... regulations around the Right to be Forgotten... are emerging... Our hope is that with a good metrics like the ones we propose and a well-defined task like TOFU, new unlearning methods are developed that push the state of the art and help imbue AI systems with the privacy that is critical for safe, and in some places legal, deployment.
